raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia who received a haploidentical stem cell transplant developed fever on post-transplant day +16. Blood culture was positive for Bacillus cereus, which was treated with vancomycin and cefepime.
On day +17, he developed a headache and became somnolent. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed a small left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions consistent with possible septic emboli, shown in Figure 1A. Magnetic resonance angiography did not show evidence of intracranial aneurysm. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no evidence of intracardiac shunt, valve disease, or vegetation. The patient was broadened to vancomycin and meropenem for treatment of presumed disseminated B. cereus. Due to persistent fever despite bloodstream clearance of B. cereus, MRI with ring-enhancing lesions, and the patient's known immunoglobulin G (IgG) seropositivity for T. gondii, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) was started empirically from days +22 to +25. This was discontinued given the negative T. gondii PCR testing from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimens. Diagnostic workup was negative for Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptococcus, and viral infection.
Given the ongoing fever, development of vomiting, and diarrhea, an endoscopy was performed on day +49. Methylprednisolone was given from day +49 to +52 for empiric management of gastrointestinal graft-vs.-host disease (GVHD), but pathology showed rare apoptotic bodies in the duodenum and colon and did not support a diagnosis of GVHD.
On day +51, the patient developed rapid-onset respiratory failure and progressive somnolence. CT scan of the chest showed diffuse ground glass opacities. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), where he developed MODS with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure and septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and significant vasoactive support. He was treated empirically with gentamicin, meropenem, TMP/SMX, amphotericin, cidofovir, albendazole, and ivermectin, with plan to start pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine when available. PCR testing of repeat BAL fluid identified T. gondii. A splenic lesion was also identified on ultrasound and biopsied, with PCR testing positive for T. gondii. All other bacterial, viral, and fungal studies were negative. TMP/SMX was dose-adjusted for the treatment of disseminated toxoplasmosis.
In addition to antimicrobials, the patient was concurrently treated with plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin for thrombocytopenia-associated multiple organ failure from day +55 to +57. Despite therapy, he developed hyperferritinemia (peak level, 49,000 ng/mL) with concurrent hepatobiliary dysfunction and coagulopathy. The results of his clinical cytokine panel from day +54 are shown in Table 1. He was also treated with anakinra based on a reanalysis of a phase III randomized trial showing a mortality benefit of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist treatment in adult severe sepsis. A timeline of his immune dysregulation and associated therapeutics is shown in Figure 2A.
Given the patient's declining respiratory status and persistent MODS despite maximal support, his family elected to discontinue life-sustaining therapy on day +58. Autopsy findings were notable for evidence of disseminated toxoplasmosis, as shown in Figure 1B. Numerous inflammatory foci and T. gondii bradyzoites were seen in the myocardium and diaphragm. Neuropathologic evaluation revealed numerous hemorrhagic subcortical infarcts containing granulomatous inflammation and T. gondii bradyzoite cysts.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia developed persistent fever on day +16, headache and somnolence on day +17, vomiting and diarrhea on day +49, and fulminant hypoxemic respiratory failure on day +51 following haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Known to be Toxoplasma gondii IgG-seropositive pre-transplant, the patient underwent a haploidentical stem cell transplant for relapsed Ph-like B-ALL and developed Bacillus cereus bacteremia on day +16 (treated with vancomycin/cefepime, then vancomycin/meropenem) followed on day +17 by headache, somnolence, a small left frontal hemorrhage on head CT, and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions on MRI. Empiric TMP/SMX was given briefly from days +22 to +25 and stopped when initial blood, CSF, and BAL T. gondii PCRs returned negative. On day +49, persistent fever, vomiting, and diarrhea prompted upper/lower endoscopy and empiric methylprednisolone (days +49 to +52) for suspected GI GVHD. On day +51, he developed rapid-onset severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, progressive somnolence, septic shock, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS).
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-like B-ALL) status post haploidentical stem cell transplantation; pre-transplant Toxoplasma gondii IgG seropositive; post-transplant day +16 Bacillus cereus bacteremia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent fever, headache, somnolence, vomiting, diarrhea, and acute respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Somnolent with headache on day +17; rapid progression on day +51 to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, septic shock, and multiorgan dysfunction requiring PICU mechanical ventilation and high-dose vasoactive support.
objective.routine_investigations: Microbiology and hyperinflammatory markers: Day +16 blood culture positive for Bacillus cereus (subsequently cleared); initial blood, CSF, and BAL negative for Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptococcus, viruses, and initial T. gondii PCR; day +55–57 profound hyperferritinemia (peak 49,000 ng/mL), hepatobiliary dysfunction, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and markedly elevated inflammatory cytokines (day +54 cytokine panel). Transthoracic echocardiogram (day +17): Normal without intracardiac shunt or vegetations.
objective.advanced_workup: Neuroimaging (day +17): Head CT showed a small left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage; brain MRI revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions (MRA negative for mycotic aneurysm). Day +49 GI endoscopy and biopsies: Rare duodenal and colonic apoptotic bodies, negative for GVHD. Day +51 chest CT, splenic ultrasound/biopsy, and repeat BAL PCR: Chest CT showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities; repeat BAL fluid PCR and ultrasound-guided splenic lesion biopsy PCR both tested positive for Toxoplasma gondii. Post-mortem autopsy (day +58): Confirmed disseminated toxoplasmosis with numerous T. gondii bradyzoites and inflammatory foci in the myocardium and diaphragm, and multiple hemorrhagic subcortical cerebral infarcts containing granulomatous inflammation and T. gondii bradyzoite cysts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal Reactivated disseminated toxoplasmosis (involving the brain, lungs, heart, diaphragm, and spleen) complicated by hyperferritinemic multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS; peak ferritin 49,000 ng/mL) following haploidentical stem cell transplantation in a T. gondii IgG-seropositive patient with Ph-like B-ALL, definitively confirmed by positive repeat BAL and splenic biopsy T. gondii PCRs and post-mortem autopsy (after false-negative day +22 blood/CSF/BAL T. gondii PCRs and negative Pneumocystis jirovecii workup). Plan and clinical course: Treated in the PICU on day +51 with mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, high-dose therapeutic TMP/SMX (plus empiric meropenem, gentamicin, amphotericin, cidofovir, albendazole, and ivermectin), plasma exchange, IVIG (days +55 to +57), and anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist). Due to refractory MODS and progressive respiratory decline, life-sustaining support was withdrawn on day +58.
